headline: A film of the Odyssey fills movie theaters

sources.title: Box Office: 'The Odyssey' Soars to $652 Million Globally After Two Weekends, Including $140 Million in Imax
'The Odyssey' extends stay in 70mm Imax theaters as shows sell out weeks in advance
Coveted 'The Odyssey' IMAX 70mm Screenings Extended After Weeks Of Sold Out Showings
'The Odyssey' drives summer box office boom through rare IMAX 70mm screenings (video, FOX 5 New York)

chunks.text: The Odyssey is a Greek [[poem]] about 2,800 years old. A film of it has become the biggest movie story of the summer. It {{came out}} on July 17, [[directed]] by Christopher Nolan with Matt Damon as Odysseus, and had {{raked in}} about 652 million dollars [[worldwide]] after only two weekends. About 140 million of that came from IMAX screens alone, which is unusual, because IMAX normally {{makes up}} a small [[share]] of any film's [[earnings]].

verbs.correct: To be released to the public
verbs.wrong: To be shown in only a few theaters
verbs.why: A new movie sequel comes out every few years, and a new phone model comes out each fall. This film based on the ancient Greek poem came out on July 17 and quickly became the biggest movie of the summer.

verbs.correct: To earn a lot of money
verbs.wrong: To spend a lot of money on ads
verbs.why: A hit movie can rake in millions in a single weekend, and a small bakery rakes in extra cash during the holidays. This film had raked in about 652 million dollars worldwide after only two weekends in theaters.

verbs.correct: To form a part of a whole
verbs.wrong: To recover money that was lost
verbs.why: Water makes up most of the human body, and imports make up a quarter of a country's total sales. IMAX screens usually make up only a small share of any film's total earnings.

chunks.text: The reason is the way it was filmed. This is the first full length film [[shot]] entirely on IMAX film cameras, using more than two million feet of [[70mm]] film. Those cameras are heavy, noisy and rare, so most directors {{stay away from}} them and film [[digitally]] instead. The reward is a picture with [[far more]] detail than an ordinary movie image, and one that fills a tall screen [[from top to bottom]] rather than filling only a wide strip across the middle.

verbs.wrong: To be unable to pay for something
verbs.why: Careful bakers stay away from cheap butter, and a cautious driver stays away from icy roads when possible. Most film directors stay away from the heavy, noisy IMAX film cameras and shoot digitally instead.

chunks.text: The problem is that [[hardly anywhere]] can show it that way. Only about 25 theaters in the whole United States can [[project]] 70mm IMAX. Seats at those [[screenings]] {{sold out}} [[as much as]] seven weeks ahead. One theater [[chain]] had to {{set up}} a digital [[waiting list]] on its app when new tickets were released. Some people flew hundreds of miles to reach a screen. On July 30 the [[studio]] {{gave in}} to the [[demand]] and [[extended]] the 70mm [[run]] by a month, to September 16.

verbs.wrong: To be offered for sale early
verbs.why: New sneakers can sell out within an hour of release, and concert tickets often sell out months before the show. Seats at the rare 70mm screenings sold out as much as seven weeks ahead.

verbs.wrong: To make a system work faster
verbs.why: A city sets up a market every Sunday, and a small team might set up a fund for young players. One theater chain set up a digital waiting list once new tickets became available.

A parent might finally give in and buy the toy after a long argument, and a company sometimes gives in to public pressure. On July 30 the studio gave in to the demand and extended the rare 70mm run by a month.

chunks.text: The money is not really the interesting part. A story that people have been {{passing down}} since before writing was even common has {{filled up}} theaters in 2026. [[Audiences]] {{lined up}} to see it in the oldest [[format]] available, not the newest one. Whether other studios now {{take up}} film cameras again is a separate question, and an expensive one, because only [[a handful of]] these cameras exist anywhere in the world.

verbs.wrong: To perform live for large audiences
verbs.why: Grandmothers pass down old recipes through the generations, and some families pass down the same stories for a hundred years. The Odyssey is a story people have been passing down since long before writing was common.

verbs.wrong: To open more screens in a city
verbs.why: A stadium fills up an hour before kickoff on game day, and city buses fill up fast during the morning rush. This ancient story has filled up movie theaters across the country during the summer of 2026.

Shoppers line up outside a store before it opens on sale day, and fans sometimes line up overnight for concert tickets. Audiences lined up to see this film in the oldest available format, not the newest one.

verbs.wrong: To take control of a company
verbs.why: A craftsman might take up an old technique his grandfather once used, and a studio could take up hand-painted sets again after years of computer graphics. Whether other studios now take up film cameras again is still an open, expensive question.

mainIdea.s: A film of an ancient Greek poem earned about 652 million dollars in its first two weekends. Because it was filmed on rare IMAX cameras, few theaters could show it, so demand forced an extension.
mainIdea.why: It had raked in 652 million dollars after two weekends, and about 140 million came from IMAX screens alone. Because only about 25 theaters could show its 70mm format, the studio extended the run to September.

mainIdea.s: An ancient Greek story became a film that took in about 652 million dollars around the world. But ticket demand was falling, so the studio shortened its rare 70mm IMAX run to end early.
mainIdea.why: Close, but demand was not falling, it was far higher than the studio expected. Seats sold out as much as seven weeks ahead, so the studio extended the run instead of cutting it short.

mainIdea.s: A large format documentary about ocean life opened in IMAX theaters last spring and earned very strongly. Only a small number of theaters worldwide could show its widest picture version at all.
mainIdea.why: This is about an earlier IMAX documentary, not the 2026 film based on the Greek poem. The article never mentions any documentary about ocean life.

lines.text: A 2,800-year-old poem is the movie hit of the summer. The Odyssey {{came out}} in July and has {{raked in}} over 650 million dollars already.
The Nolan film? I heard tickets are impossible.
On the special screens, yes. Seats {{sold out}} seven weeks ahead, and one chain had to {{set up}} a waiting list on its app. Some fans flew hundreds of miles for a seat.
What's so special about the screens?

It's the first full movie shot entirely on IMAX film cameras. Most directors {{stay away from}} them, they're heavy, noisy, and rare. But the picture fills the whole tall screen with incredible detail.
How many theaters can even show that?
About 25 in the whole United States. IMAX normally {{makes up}} a small share of a film's earnings, but here it's 140 million.
So what did the studio do about the demand?
It {{gave in}} and extended the special run by a month.
There's something beautiful about this, no? The oldest story winning in the oldest format.
That's the part I love. A story people have been {{passing down}} since before writing was common has {{filled up}} theaters in 2026, and audiences {{lined up}} for film, not digital.
Will other directors {{take up}} film cameras again?
[[That's the expensive question]]. Only a handful of those cameras exist in the world.
Homer, [[still killing it]] after almost three thousand years.
